cards.front: {{c1::Evidence}} is information from observations or measurements that supports or argues against an idea.
cards.quote: Evidence is information from observations or measurements that supports or argues against an idea.

cards.front: A group of living things is {{c1::extinct}} when no living members are left.
cards.quote: A group is extinct when no living members are left.

cards.front: Trilobites are found in western Virginia rocks. What kind of animals were they, and what does finding them show?
cards.back: They were extinct sea animals with hard shells. Their fossils show that a kind of life existed that is not alive now.
cards.quote: Trilobites, extinct sea animals with hard shells, are found in western Virginia rocks.

cards.front: Sea shells are found in Virginia's coastal plain. What do they show about that land long ago?
cards.back: A shallow sea once covered the land. Fossils can show what the environment was like, not only what lived there.
cards.quote: Sea shells in Virginia's coastal plain show that a shallow sea once covered that land.

cards.front: Virginia's state fossil scallop looks much like a living scallop. What pattern in the fossil record does this show?
cards.back: Change. Old forms look like, but are not the same as, living ones.
cards.quote: Old forms look like, but are not the same as, living ones.

cards.front: The oldest fossil found so far of a fish group (Haikouichthys) is about 518 million years old. Does that show the exact day the group began?
cards.back: No. It shows only that the group existed by then. Some groups have older fossils, and new finds can push dates back.
cards.quote: No. It shows that the group existed by then.

cards.front: A {{c1::common ancestor}} is an early population that two or more kinds of living things came from.
cards.quote: A common ancestor is an early population that two or more kinds of living things came from.

cards.front: A cat leg, a whale flipper and a bat wing have the same set of bones in different shapes and jobs. Why does a shared ancestor explain this best?
cards.back: Inherited changes can reshape an old set of parts. A shared ancestor with that bone map explains why the same parts appear in different shapes.
cards.quote: Inherited changes can reshape an old set of parts, so a shared ancestor with this bone map explains the match best.

cards.front: A butterfly wing and a bird wing both fly, but only the bird wing has bones. Does the shared job show they are close relatives?
cards.back: No. The job is alike, but the build is different. Scientists compare how parts are built and where they sit.
cards.quote: No. The job is alike, but the build is different.

cards.front: A DNA {{c1::sequence}} is the order of the bases A, T, C and G along a piece of DNA.
cards.quote: A DNA sequence is the order of the bases A, T, C and G along a piece of DNA.

cards.front: Two animals make the same protein, but it differs at some positions. Where does that difference come from?
cards.back: From a difference in the DNA of the gene that carries the code for the protein.
cards.quote: so a protein difference comes from a difference in its gene's DNA

cards.front: Why does "closer relatives usually have more similar sequences" say "usually" and not "always"?
cards.back: Changes do not build up at one steady rate, and one short protein is not a complete family tree.
cards.quote: changes do not build up at one steady rate, and one short protein is not a complete family tree

cards.front: In the cytochrome c data, the horse protein differs from the human protein at 12 of 104 positions. At how many positions do the two proteins match?
cards.back: 104 - 12 = 92 positions match. The 12 counts differences, and 104 is every position compared.
cards.quote: The table counts how many of its 104 positions differ from the human protein.

cards.front: Cytochrome c differences from the human protein: rhesus monkey 1, mouse 9, dog 11, chicken 13, rattlesnake 15 (out of 104). Based only on this protein, which animal is the closest relative of humans, and which differs most?
cards.back: The rhesus monkey is closest because it differs at the fewest positions. The rattlesnake differs most. This pattern fits common ancestry.
cards.quote: Not counting humans, chimpanzee and rhesus monkey differ least; the rattlesnake differs most.

cards.front: The chimpanzee cytochrome c protein shows 0 differences from the human protein. Does that mean chimpanzee and human DNA are the same everywhere?
cards.back: No. The table compares one small protein, not the whole genome. Other genes should be checked too.
cards.quote: This table compares one small protein, not the whole genome.

cards.front: The chicken differs from the human cytochrome c protein at 13 positions and the rattlesnake at 15. Is a gap of two enough to decide which is closer to humans?
cards.back: No. Birds and snakes split from our line at the same branch point, so they are equally related to us. One short protein is not a complete family tree.
cards.quote: changes do not build up at one steady rate, and one short protein is not a complete family tree

cards.front: A {{c1::hypothesis}} is a possible explanation that a test can support or reject.
cards.quote: A hypothesis is a possible explanation that a test can support or reject.
cards.section: Why scientists call it a theory

cards.front: A student says evolution is "just a theory." What does theory mean in science?
cards.back: A well-tested explanation backed by many lines of evidence. It is not a guess, and it makes predictions that can be checked.
cards.quote: Key idea: A scientific theory is a well-tested explanation.
cards.section: Why scientists call it a theory

cards.front: Fossils, body structures and sequences could each have told a different story. What do their broad patterns show instead, and what do scientists do when details conflict?
cards.back: Their broad patterns largely agree. When details conflict, scientists check more evidence.
cards.quote: Each could have told a different story. Instead, their broad patterns largely agree; when details conflict, scientists check more evidence.
cards.section: Why scientists call it a theory

cards.front: Which remains are more likely to become fossils, and what helps?
cards.back: Hard remains, such as shells, buried fast. Soft remains left unburied usually rot first, so the fossil record has gaps.
cards.quote: Hard remains and fast burial make fossils more likely.
cards.section: Design problem: model burial and decay

cards.front: In a model of burial and decay, apple slices are buried in damp sand or laid unburied on the same damp sand, and rot is scored after 7 days. Why add clean shells to both groups?
cards.back: As a hard-part check. Shells should barely change in either group; hard remains make fossils more likely.
cards.quote: Add clean shells to both groups as a hard-part check.
cards.section: Design problem: model burial and decay

cards.front: In the burial model, buried apple slices score less rotten than unburied slices. What does this show, and what does it leave out?
cards.back: Burial slowed decay in this model. It leaves out what real fossils need: fast burial in fine mud with little oxygen and no scavengers.
cards.quote: Real fossils form best when remains are buried fast in fine mud with little oxygen and no scavengers, which this model leaves out.
cards.section: Design problem: model burial and decay

cards.front: A student says a seal and a fish are close relatives because both have fins and swim. What evidence would you check, and why is the shared job not enough?
cards.back: Check how the parts are built and where they sit, and compare protein or DNA sequences. The job is alike, but the build can be different.
cards.quote: No. The job is alike, but the build is different.

cards.front: Bone comparisons suggest animal A is closest to B, but a protein comparison suggests A is closest to C. What should scientists do, and why?
cards.back: Check more evidence. No single fossil, limb or protein settles every relationship.
cards.quote: No single fossil, limb or protein settles every relationship.
